title: No fixed mind
hook: the sage has no fixed mind and is good even to those who are not good (Tao Te Ching 49)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was daily decrease: learning adds every day, and the way subtracts every day. Your line was less each day.

The neighbor who never waves back. The relative who turns every holiday into a debate. The driver who cuts across two lanes and then glares at you. A quiet rule runs under a lot of daily life: be good to people who are good to you, and give the others what they give. It feels fair. Chapter forty-nine of the Tao Te Ching describes someone who doesn't keep that rule, and starts by saying this person has no fixed mind.
screen: `THE NEIGHBOR WHO NEVER WAVES.` → `GIVE WHAT YOU GET.` → `SOMEONE WHO DOESN'T KEEP THE RULE.`

segments.voice: First, the opening. In James Legge's translation: "The sage has no invariable mind of his own; he makes the mind of the people his mind." No fixed mind doesn't mean no opinions. It means not walking in with a verdict already decided, and letting other people's lives and needs shape how you see. Second, the hard line. Legge again: "To those who are good (to me), I am good; and to those who are not good (to me), I am also good." The same goes for trust: the sage is sincere with the sincere, and with the insincere too. The reason given is that goodness spreads this way. Kindness that waits for kindness first is a trade. Kindness given anyway changes what happens next. Third, what this isn't. The chapter describes a way of meeting people, not a duty to stay in harm's way. Being good to someone can mean a calm word, a fair deal, or a door held open, while still keeping a safe distance. Good to all is about the heart you bring, not about letting anyone hurt you. If someone is hurting you, your safety comes first: in the US you can call or text 988 at any hour, and wherever you are, local emergency help is there. Fourth, the ending. The sage treats people the way a parent treats children. Children aren't kind every minute either, and a parent doesn't reset the whole relationship after one rude remark. Chapter forty-nine asks for that steadiness with the neighbor, the relative, the driver. Not a fixed mind. An open one.
screen: `NO INVARIABLE MIND OF HIS OWN.` · `GOOD TO THOSE WHO ARE NOT GOOD.` · `NOT A DUTY TO STAY IN HARM'S WAY.` · `LIKE A PARENT WITH CHILDREN.` · then, large: `NO FIXED MIND.`

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind who hasn't been good to you lately, someone you can safely think about, and notice the verdict you've already reached about them. Set it down, just for these two minutes. If you pray, you might hold them in your prayer; if you don't, wish them one simple good thing: rest, a better day, a kind word from someone.
No fixed mind. Chapter forty-nine: the sage has no invariable mind, and is good to those who are good, and good to those who are not. Today's word.
Your line: good to all. Steady, the way a parent stays steady. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1111 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: NO PLACE FOR THE TIGER.`

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter forty-nine as a model for meeting difficult people with steady goodwill, without first deciding who they are, while still keeping themselves safe.

chat.says: Does being good to everyone mean putting up with people who hurt you?
options: No; it's about the heart you bring, not a duty to stay in harm's way.
Yes; the chapter says to stay close to anyone who mistreats you, always.
No; it says be good only to those who have been good to you first.
chat.meaning: Chapter forty-nine: the sage is good to the good and to the not good. This lesson adds that it's no duty to stay in harm's way.

notes: Editor: replaced the stock 'an ordinary Tuesday' frame; Legge's two quotations of ch. 49 checked.
